article_title: Co-Designing New Approaches to School Safety
citation: Johnson, D.W. (2026). Co-designing new approaches to school safety: District and community perspectives on Chicago's Whole School Safety Framework. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Four key features of the WSS co-design model: inclusive design, restorative orientation, addressing institutional harm, and demonstrated possibility
description: The interpretive summary distills the co-design process into four key features participants highlighted as it evolved into a template for future efforts. "Inclusive design: The process intentionally centered diverse perspectives—students, families, community members, and district staff—in shaping policy." The restorative orientation was grounded in "relationship-building, trust, and reciprocal accountability," and the process was seen as evidence that authentic collaboration is feasible and replicable in other contexts.
requirements: Sustained participatory structures such as a steering committee including district staff and community-based organizations with their constituencies
constraints: The article notes sustaining this degree of partnership amid leadership turnover at CPS and the CBOE is a defining challenge as WSS scales from framework to policy to practice
target_learners: students and families in school communities
examples: Between December 2020 and January 2021, CPS and CBO leaders co-designed common questions for CBO-led public meetings held in February 2021, then synthesized learnings into consensus recommendations shared with the CBOE on March 24, 2021
key_sources: Johnson, D.W. (2026). Co-designing new approaches to school safety: District and community perspectives on Chicago's Whole School Safety Framework. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/co-designing-new-approaches-to-school-safety

article_title: Supporting California's Children through a Whole Child Approach: A Field Guide for Creating Integrated, School-Based Systems of Care
citation: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions
title: Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child (WSCC) model
description: The WSCC model, from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, "aims to align the work of the public health and education sectors—which often serve the same students and share the same goals" so schools can adopt a whole child approach. It categorizes programs and services into 10 components: physical education and physical activity; nutrition environment and services; health education; social and emotional climate; physical environment; health services; counseling, psychological, and social services; employee wellness; community involvement; and family engagement. The guide uses it as an organizing framework, mapping local strategies (e.g., Solano County's school-based wellness centers) onto its components.
requirements: Families and communities must act as critical partners with education professionals, as the model emphasizes
constraints: The guide notes frameworks vary widely and there is no consensus in the field on how whole child frameworks relate to one another
target_learners: All K-12 students, with families and communities as partners
target_learning_goals: Student health, learning, and development through coordinated health and education services
examples: The Solano County Takin' CLAS to the Schools strategy is described as reflecting the family engagement, community involvement, health education, and counseling components of the WSCC model
key_sources: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions

article_title: The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students
citation: Lewallen TC, Hunt H, Potts-Datema W, Zaza S, Giles W. (2015). The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students. Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.12310
title: The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child (WSCC) model: a unified socioecological framework integrating health and education
description: The WSCC model is a conceptual framework developed jointly by ASCD and CDC that combines the Whole Child approach and the coordinated school health approach. The article states that "The WSCC model is designed to provide a shared framework and approach for decision making and action for both sectors to work together." It places the student at the center, surrounds the child with a ring stressing coordination among policy, process, and practice, and an outer ring of school health components emphasizing the school as part of the community. The authors describe it as a socioecological approach directed at the whole school, drawing resources from the whole community.
requirements: Coordination among policy, process, and practice; administrator support, particularly principals, for integration of learning and health
constraints: The article states the model is a framework and not an intervention; specific interventions, curricula, and classroom practices depend on local context
target_learning_goals: Educational attainment and healthy development; students healthy, safe, engaged, supported, and challenged
examples: Developed through spring 2013 expert panel meetings convened by ASCD and CDC, with outcomes vetted by a review group of stakeholders
key_sources: Lewallen TC, Hunt H, Potts-Datema W, Zaza S, Giles W. (2015). The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students. Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.12310

article_title: The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students
citation: Lewallen TC, Hunt H, Potts-Datema W, Zaza S, Giles W. (2015). The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students. Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.12310
title: WSCC model's expanded and renamed school health components (10-component outer ring)
description: The WSCC model's outer ring incorporates and revises the CSH components. The article reports that "the healthy and safe school environment component is now separated into “social and emotional climate” and “physical environment” giving greater attention to each," that family and community involvement is split into community involvement and family engagement, that health promotion for staff becomes employee wellness, and that nutrition services and physical education are expanded to include the nutrition environment and physical activity. Definitions for each component were developed by subject matter experts and vetted with experts in the field.
requirements: Component definitions vetted with experts in the field; qualified, trained staff for components such as health education and physical education
target_learning_goals: Health literacy, health-promoting decision making, and academic success supported by a healthy school environment
examples: The nutrition services component expanded to include the nutrition environment; physical education expanded to include physical activity
key_sources: Lewallen TC, Hunt H, Potts-Datema W, Zaza S, Giles W. (2015). The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students. Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.12310

article_title: Debate Instruction in EFL Classroom: Impacts on the Critical Thinking and Speaking Skill
citation: Iman, J. N. (2017). Debate Instruction in EFL Classroom: Impacts on the Critical Thinking and Speaking Skill. International Journal of Instruction, 10(4), 87-108. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2017.1046a
title: World Schools Debating Championship (WSDC) format as implemented in the study
description: The WSDC format is a structured classroom debate system in which "There are 2 teams debating, each consists of 3 (three) debaters" on Government/Affirmative and Opposition/Negative sides. Each speaker delivers an 8-minute substantive speech followed by 4-minute reply speeches, with points of information (POIs) allowed between the 1st and 7th minute. Teams receive 30 minutes preparation time without outside help or devices, and an odd number of judges decides the winner. The study used this format as the experimental treatment across 21 teaching sessions of 90 minutes.
requirements: A chairperson and time keeper must be selected; ideally the teacher acts as chairperson for the first debate activity
constraints: During preparation time teams are not allowed help from anybody or use of laptops, PDAs, or communication devices
target_learners: tenth-grade senior high school EFL students
examples: The experimental group received the WSDC treatment across 21 teaching sessions, each lasting 90 minutes, excluding pretest and posttest
key_sources: Iman, J. N. (2017). Debate Instruction in EFL Classroom: Impacts on the Critical Thinking and Speaking Skill. International Journal of Instruction, 10(4), 87-108. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2017.1046a

article_title: Debate Instruction in EFL Classroom: Impacts on the Critical Thinking and Speaking Skill
citation: Iman, J. N. (2017). Debate Instruction in EFL Classroom: Impacts on the Critical Thinking and Speaking Skill. International Journal of Instruction, 10(4), 87-108. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2017.1046a
title: Thirteen-step classroom debate instructional procedure from teacher explanation to summary
description: The article enumerates an instructional procedure for running WSDC debate in class: the teacher explains the technique, presents the motion, divides the class into Proposition and Opposition teams, selects three debaters per side plus chairperson and time keeper, arranges positions, runs the debate with alternating speeches and reply speeches, closes it, and then "the teacher asks the student to explain the summary of debate" before teacher and students conclude the learning materials. The motion for the next meeting is announced in advance.
requirements: The teacher must first explain the objective, components, outline, and rules of debate and how to debate
examples: In the study the procedure was applied in the experimental group as the English teaching activity for one session of lesson across 21 teaching sessions
key_sources: Iman, J. N. (2017). Debate Instruction in EFL Classroom: Impacts on the Critical Thinking and Speaking Skill. International Journal of Instruction, 10(4), 87-108. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2017.1046a

article_title: The Effects of Webopac Self Training Tool with Guided Exploration on Information Literacy Skills among First Year Degree Students
citation: Mohd Nasir Ismail, Nurfaezah Mamat, Adnan Jamaludin. (2018). The Effects of Webopac Self Training Tool with Guided Exploration on Information Literacy Skills among First Year Degree Students. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: WSTTG instructional design grounded in Ausubel's Instructional Design Theory and Gagne's Nine Events of Instruction
description: The WebOPAC Self Training Tool with Guided Exploration (WSTTG) is a web-based self-training tool plus a self-guided manual for teaching library catalogue (WebOPAC) use. Its instructional design was "developed according to Ausebel’s Instructional Design Theory and Gagne‘s Nine Events of Instruction which consist of constructivist learning environment model and cognitive of multimedia learning model." The article states the strategy "is used to develop individual’s logical thinking skill and access the information literacy sk ills" aligned with ACRL Information Literacy Competency Standards and Bloom Taxonomy. It is the guided-exploration analogue of the otherwise identical non-guided WSTT tool.
requirements: Complies with ACRL Information Literacy Competency Standards for Higher Education and Bloom Taxonomy standard
Delivered through a WebOPAC web based self-training tool together with a self-guided manual
constraints: Developed and evaluated for first-year degree students in Malaysian public university library orientation contexts
target_learners: first year degree students in Malaysian public universities
target_learning_goals: information literacy skills for using WebOPAC
examples: The study trained students via WSTTG, WSTT and T groups in library orientation sessions at three UiTM campuses and assessed outcomes with the WTAILS posttest.
key_sources: Mohd Nasir Ismail, Nurfaezah Mamat, Adnan Jamaludin. (2018). The Effects of Webopac Self Training Tool with Guided Exploration on Information Literacy Skills among First Year Degree Students. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1165734

article_title: Enhancing academic performance and student engagement in health education: insights from Work Station Learning Activities (WSLA).
citation: Sánchez Judit, Lesmes Marta, Rubio Margarita, Gal Beatriz, Tutor Antonio S. (2024). Enhancing academic performance and student engagement in health education: insights from Work Station Learning Activities (WSLA). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05478-z
title: Work Station Learning Activities (WSLA): five-step workstation-based active learning methodology for integrated basic science teaching
description: WSLA is a flexible and scalable teaching tool for progressively integrating basic science subjects into the biomedical curriculum, described as teaching "a particular topic (e.g. pH regulation) across a series of different workstations run in a clinical scenario." Its five steps are: pre-session content on virtual campus, a pre-test, presentation of a clinical scenario with workstations and team-based worksheets, a general review with assessment, and a post-test. In this study three 2-hour WSLA sessions integrated Biochemistry/Physiology and Anatomy/Physiology content for first-year medical students.
requirements: Pre-session content provision and a pre-test to ensure student readiness before the hands-on session
Team-based worksheet activities at each workstation solved as a group
constraints: Aligned with the correlation level of Harden's Integration Ladder, i.e., discipline-based instruction with integrated teaching alongside, not a fully integrated curriculum
target_learning_goals: integrating basic science concepts with clinical application
teamwork and collaborative reasoning in clinical scenarios
examples: Session 1 integrated pH regulation (Biochemistry and Physiology); session 2 addressed carpal tunnel syndrome and session 3 radiculopathy (Anatomy and Physiology), each lasting 2 hours
key_sources: Sánchez Judit, Lesmes Marta, Rubio Margarita, Gal Beatriz, Tutor Antonio S. (2024). Enhancing academic performance and student engagement in health education: insights from Work Station Learning Activities (WSLA). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05478-z
